probes.intro: A short fable about two animals who invite each other to dinner.

items.stem: What did the Fox give the Stork for dinner?
options: Food in a jar with a long neck
Soup in a very shallow dish
Fish on a large plate
Bread in a basket
items.rationale: The Fox “put nothing before her but some soup in a very shallow dish.”

items.stem: Why could the Fox not eat at the Stork’s house?
options: He did not like the soup
The Stork had eaten all of the food before he came
He was too full from his own dinner
His snout would not fit into the narrow jar
items.rationale: The dinner was in a jar “in which the Fox could not insert his snout.”

items.stem: What does the Stork mean when she says, “One bad turn deserves another”?
options: She tricked the Fox because he tricked her first
She is sorry that her dinner went badly
She wants the Fox to cook her a better dinner next time
Friends should always share their food
items.rationale: The Fox served the soup “for a joke” that the Stork could not eat, so she served a dinner the Fox could not reach.

probes.intro: A science writer explains how honeybees keep the air in their hive fresh.

items.stem: Why does the air inside the hive need to be moved?
options: Rain has come in through the open windows of the hive
The honey has started to spoil
The crowded bees make it hot and the air bad
The bees want to go outside to play
items.rationale: Where “so many insects are packed closely together the heat will become very great, and the air impure and unwholesome.”

items.stem: The bees wave their wings to make “a current of air.” What is a current of air?
options: Air that is moving along
Air that smells sweet like honey
A loud buzzing sound
A small cloud of dust
items.rationale: The bees wave their wings “to and fro, producing a current of air,” and so “air is sent into all the passages.”

items.stem: Why do more bees stand all over the floor of the hive, fanning with their backs to the entrance?
options: To keep the honey collectors from coming in
To cool the honey before it is stored
To guard the hive from other insects
To send the fresh air farther into the hive
items.rationale: Together with the bees at the entrance they fan, “and in this way air is sent into all the passages.”

probes.intro: A nature-study writer explains that a sunflower head is really made of many small flowers.

items.stem: What job do the ray, or “banner,” flowers do?
options: They make the seeds
They keep the buds in the middle safe from the rain
They store food for the winter
They attract insects with their bright petals
items.rationale: The ray flowers “hold out bright pennants to attract the attention of insects.”

items.stem: Why does the author call the composite plan “a plan of flower cooperation”?
options: Sunflowers grow best beside other plants
Many small flowers work together as one flower-head
Insects help children study the flowers
Each garden flower blooms at a different time of year
items.rationale: In this plan “there are many flowers associated to form a single flower-head.”

items.stem: The author calls the garden sunflower “the teacher’s ally.” What does ally mean here?
options: A helper
An enemy
A student
A garden path
items.rationale: The sunflower helps “illustrate to the children the story of the composites” because its florets are so large.

items.stem: How is studying composite flowers different from usual nature-study, according to the author?
options: You need to study them only in spring
You need a microscope to see any part
You need to study the single florets one by one
You need a botanist to pull them apart for you
items.rationale: “Ordinarily, in nature-study we do not pull the flowers apart,” but with composites “it is necessary to study the individual florets.”

probes.intro: A nature-study writer describes what she noticed about frogs’ colors, eyes, and ears.

items.stem: How is this passage organized?
options: One part on color, one on eyes, and one on ears
It follows one frog’s life from egg to grown adult
It gives the steps for catching a frog
It compares frogs with fish and birds
items.rationale: The paragraphs move from the frog’s color to “The eyes of frogs” and then to “The ear.”

items.stem: Why is it useful for a frog to be green while a toad is the color of soil?
options: Green frogs are easier for enemies to find
Toads are older than frogs
Each one matches the place where it lives
Frogs need more sunlight than toads
items.rationale: “the frog lives among green things, while it is to the toad’s advantage to be the color of the soil.”

items.stem: “When the frog winks, the nictitating membrane rises from below and covers the whole eye.” What is the nictitating membrane?
options: The colored ring around the dark middle of the eye
The flat round ear behind the eye
A gold spot on the frog’s back
A thin covering that can close over the eye
items.rationale: It “rises from below and covers the whole eye” when the frog winks.

items.stem: Why does a leopard frog hiding at the bottom of the aquarium let its eyelids fall?
options: Because it is falling asleep
So its eyes will not shine and give it away
So it can change the color of its shining eyes
So it can hear better under water
items.rationale: It covers its eyes “so that they do not shine up and attract pursuers.”

probes.intro: In this chapter of a novel, Mary has just met Dickon, the brother of Martha, who works in the house. Martha speaks a Yorkshire dialect: “tha” means “you.”

items.stem: Why does Mary keep praising Dickon’s turned-up nose, round eyes, and big mouth?
options: She is teasing Martha by pretending she likes how he looks
She agrees that Dickon is not handsome
She admires him and won’t let Martha’s doubts change that
She wants Martha to stop talking about him
items.rationale: Mary answers each of Martha’s doubts with praise: “I like it to turn up” and “I like them round.”

items.stem: “I love his big mouth,” said Mary obstinately. What does obstinately mean?
options: Stubbornly, refusing to give way
Shyly, in a quiet voice
Sadly, as if about to cry
Jokingly, as if she does not mean it
items.rationale: Mary keeps defending each feature after Martha’s doubts, ending with “I wish mine were just like it.”

items.stem: Whom does Martha advise Mary to ask for a place to plant the seeds?
options: Mr. Roach, the head gardener
Ben Weatherstaff
Mr. Craven
Dickon
items.rationale: Martha says, “If I was you, I'd ask Ben Weatherstaff.”

items.stem: Why is Mary frightened when Martha asks where the flowers will be planted?
options: She has lost the seeds Dickon brought
She does not know how to use the tools
She thinks Martha wants to use the seeds in her own garden
She has no permission and fears she may not get a place
items.rationale: Mary admits, “I haven't asked anybody yet,” and anxiously hopes no one could “mind my having it.”

probes.intro: In this retelling of a Greek myth, the heroes of the ship Argo sail into an unknown sea.

items.stem: Why were the heroes afraid as they sailed into the Black Sea?
options: Their ship had been badly damaged in a storm on the way
No Greek had crossed it, and strange stories were told of it
Orpheus had told them that the goddess Hera was against them
They had run out of food and water
items.rationale: “No Hellen had ever crossed it,” and people “told strange stories of it.”

items.stem: Tiphys is called “the cunning helmsman.” What does cunning mean here?
options: Dishonest and sly
Frightened and weak
Proud and boastful
Skillful and clever
items.rationale: Tiphys watches until he can follow the heron, which he calls “the cunning bird,” through the one gap.

items.stem: Why does Tiphys stand silent before steering between the rocks?
options: He has decided to turn the ship around
He is angry with Orpheus for frightening the crew
He is watching for a sign of a safe way through
He is waiting for the rocks to sink
items.rationale: He stood silent “till he saw a heron” that seemed to be “looking for a passage through,” then followed it.

items.stem: Why does the author say the rocks struck “but a feather from his tail”?
options: To show how narrowly the heron escaped
To show that the heron was badly hurt
To explain why the heron left the ship
To show that the rocks were made of glass
items.rationale: The rocks “clashed together as the bird fled swiftly through,” missing it by only a feather.

probes.intro: A nineteenth-century country writer describes something strange he saw one summer evening after a day of rain.

items.stem: What first made the writer go back and look through the gap again?
options: A rabbit came out from behind a bush near the gap
He heard the sound of a steam plough at work on the hill
The rain suddenly began again
The hill looked far higher than he had ever noticed
items.rationale: That part of the hills looked “remarkably high,” and it seemed “singular” that he had never noticed it.

items.stem: What made the hill look like a mountain?
options: A dark cloud resting on it had taken its exact shape
Rain had washed away the hedges around it
Smoke from a steam plough at work had piled up above it
The setting sun lit the hill from below
items.rationale: “Upon the central hill a cloud was resting, and had for the time taken its exact shape.”

items.stem: Why did climbing onto the mound show him the cause?
options: The cloud lifted off the hill as soon as he climbed onto the mound
From up there the barn and the clump of trees looked much smaller
He saw the whole range, with the hills on each side at normal height
The mound was higher than the hill itself
items.rationale: From the mound “the whole range of hills could be seen,” and the down to “right and left remained still at its former level.”

items.stem: “nor could the eye separate the hill from the unsubstantial vapour.” What does unsubstantial mean here?
options: Very dark
Not solid
Slow-moving
Dangerous
items.rationale: The vapour is cloud, which later lifted and “slowly sailed eastwards with the wind,” unlike the solid hill.

probes.intro: A nineteenth-century country writer describes how birds travel to an orchard on a farm.

items.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Birds use certain hedges as regular routes to favorite places
The orchard at Wick grows the best apples and damsons nearby
Finches are the only birds that ever visit the orchard at Wick
Hedges should be cut back to keep birds away
items.rationale: The hedge is “a favourite highway of birds and other wild creatures, and leads direct to the orchard.”

items.stem: The writer calls the hedge a “highway” and a “caravan route.” What do these comparisons suggest?
options: The hedge is noisy and dangerous
Many travellers use the same path again and again
The birds travel only at night
People planted the hedge long ago to help birds travel
items.rationale: Birds are “constantly passing up or down it,” as travellers use a road.

items.stem: Which detail best shows that birds prefer this hedge in particular?
options: The hedge holds hazel, willow, and maple
A little stream runs down the ditch
Greenfinches travel along it in pairs, calling softly
A parallel hedge 150 yards away is nearly deserted
items.rationale: Another hedge nearby “is comparatively deserted,” and there “You may wait there in vain and see nothing but a robin.”

items.stem: “their contented notes gradually become inaudible as they go towards the orchard.” What does inaudible mean?
options: Louder and much clearer
Sad and lonely
Too faint to be heard
Out of tune
items.rationale: The finches are moving away “towards the orchard,” so their calls fade until they cannot be heard.

probes.intro: Frederick Douglass, then enslaved in Baltimore, had been badly beaten by workers at Mr. Gardner’s shipyard. Calking means sealing the seams of a ship.

items.stem: “Master Hugh, finding he could get no redress, refused to let me go back again to Mr. Gardner.” What does redress mean here?
options: A new set of work clothes
Permission to leave the city of Baltimore
A remedy or payment for a wrong
An apology from Douglass
items.rationale: Douglass had been hurt at Gardner’s yard, so “his wife dressed my wound,” and Hugh could get nothing to set that wrong right.

items.stem: How did Douglass’s working life change after he learned to calk?
options: He worked only for Master Hugh, who also set all his wages
He found his own jobs and contracts and collected his pay
He earned less than the other calkers
He was sent back to Mr. Gardner’s shipyard
items.rationale: “I sought my own employment, made my own contracts, and collected the money which I earned.”

items.stem: What does Douglass conclude about how better conditions affected him?
options: They made him content to remain enslaved
They made him forget about freedom
They made him trust Master Hugh and want to please him
They made him want freedom more, not feel content
items.rationale: “whenever my condition was improved, instead of its increasing my contentment, it only increased my desire to be free.”

items.stem: Why does Douglass list “Not because he earned it,—not because he had any hand in earning it”?
options: To rule out every justification, leaving only force
To show that Master Hugh helped him earn the money
To explain how wages in the shipyard were calculated each week
To admit that he was unsure why he paid
items.rationale: After the list he concludes that Hugh took the money “solely because he had the power to compel me to give it up.”

probes.intro: Benjamin Franklin recalls teaching himself languages as an adult. His eighteenth-century spellings, such as “us'd” for “used,” are kept.

items.stem: How did Franklin and his acquaintance use chess to study Italian?
options: They spoke only Italian to each other while they played
The winner of each game set the loser a study task
The loser paid for the winner’s lessons
They stopped playing chess altogether
items.rationale: “the victor in every game should have a right to impose a task” of grammar or translation.

items.stem: Why did Franklin understand more Latin than he expected?
options: He had studied Latin for many years as a boy
The Latin Testament included a translation
His chess partner had been secretly teaching him Latin
French, Italian, and Spanish had prepared him for it
items.rationale: He found he did better because “those preceding languages had greatly smooth'd my way.”

items.stem: In Franklin’s staircase comparison, what do the lowest steps stand for?
options: Modern languages, such as French
Greek, an older language than Latin
Latin, which he says should come first
Lessons for very young children
items.rationale: He argues “if you begin with the lowest you will with more ease ascend to the top,” then proposes beginning with French.

items.stem: What does Franklin suggest to those in charge of educating young people?
options: Begin with Greek so that learning Latin is easier later
Stop teaching languages to most students
Consider teaching modern languages before Latin
Use games like chess to teach Latin
items.rationale: He asks whether “it would not have been better to have begun with the French, proceeding to the Italian.”

probes.intro: In this section of an 1837 address, Ralph Waldo Emerson describes nature as the first influence on a scholar’s mind. Bracketed numbers are reference marks from the printed edition.

items.stem: According to the passage, how does a young mind’s understanding of nature develop?
options: It learns general laws first, then notices each separate thing
It studies books first, then turns to nature
It classifies things, then forgets the classes
It sees things as separate, then joins them under shared laws
items.rationale: “To the young mind everything is individual,” but “By and by it finds how to join two things and see in them one nature.”

items.stem: “The ambitious soul sits down before each refractory fact.” What does refractory mean here?
options: Bending light, as a lens or prism does
Recently discovered by science
Stubborn; hard to explain or classify
Of little importance to the mind
items.rationale: The soul “reduces all strange constitutions, all new powers, to their class and their law,” so a refractory fact is one that resists that order.

items.stem: Of nature and the soul, Emerson writes, “One is seal and one is print.” What relationship does this image express?
options: They match part for part, like a stamp and its mark
Nature is a book that the soul must print and read
The soul is sealed away from nature and cannot touch it
Nature copies the soul, but poorly
items.rationale: Just before the image he says nature is the soul’s opposite, “answering to it part for part.”

items.stem: What does Emerson conclude in the final sentences?
options: Science should replace the study of the self
Studying nature and knowing oneself become one task
Nature can never be understood by the mind
Ancient wisdom matters more than modern science does
items.rationale: The precepts “Know thyself” and “Study nature” “become at last one maxim.”

probes.intro: In this chapter of Walden (1854), Henry David Thoreau writes about books and what it means to read well.

items.stem: What does Thoreau claim about real reading in the final paragraph?
options: It is demanding work for our most alert hours
It should give way to direct experience
It matters less than knowing how to keep accounts
It is easy once a person knows the alphabet
items.rationale: True reading is “what we have to stand on tiptoe to read and devote our most alert and wakeful hours to.”

items.stem: Thoreau says most people read the great poets “as the multitude read the stars, at most astrologically, not astronomically.” What does this suggest?
options: They read poetry only at night, by the light of the stars
They prefer the science of astronomy to reading poetry
They read only poems about the stars
They read for fanciful meanings, not with careful study
items.rationale: He contrasts such reading with reading as “a noble intellectual exercise,” of which most men “know little or nothing.”

items.stem: Why, according to Thoreau, does the wealthy trader work to give his children intellectual culture?
options: He wants his children to become traders too
He feels his riches cannot replace the culture he lacks
He has read the classics himself and wants to share them
Society requires it of every wealthy family
items.rationale: The trader feels “the vanity and insufficiency of all his riches” and the culture “whose want he so keenly feels.”

items.stem: “Most men have learned to read to serve a paltry convenience.” What does paltry mean?
options: Generous and helpful
Ancient and respected
Small and unimportant
Strict and required
items.rationale: Thoreau sets this use beside learning “to cipher in order to keep accounts,” a minor aim next to reading as “a noble intellectual exercise.”

probes.intro: In this dialogue from Plato’s Republic (Benjamin Jowett’s translation), Socrates, who narrates (“I said”), discusses with Glaucon what young people should study.

items.stem: Socrates says geometry concerns them if it “compels us to view being,” but not if it shows “becoming only.” What does becoming mean here?
options: What is attractive or suitable
What is still being proved
What changes and passes away
What is useful in war
items.rationale: He soon sets “the eternal” against what is “perishing and transient.”

items.stem: What does Socrates argue is the main reason to study geometry?
options: It draws the soul toward knowledge of the eternal
It teaches generals how to arrange their armies in battle
It prepares people for trade and accounts
It is the easiest science to learn
items.rationale: “geometry will draw the soul toward truth, and create the spirit of philosophy.”

items.stem: Why does Socrates call the usual language of geometricians “narrow and ridiculous”?
options: They use words that are too difficult for young students
They refuse to apply geometry to war
They argue among themselves about every proof they make
They treat geometry as practical work, not as knowledge
items.rationale: They “confuse the necessities of geometry with those of daily life; whereas knowledge is the real object of the whole science.”

items.stem: What is the role of Socrates’s closing mention of geometry’s “indirect effects”?
options: It takes back his earlier argument about the soul
It admits practical benefits but ranks them second
It shows that Glaucon’s military reason is the main one
It introduces a new subject, arithmetic
items.rationale: He names “the military advantages of which you spoke” only after the main argument, as effects that are “indirect.”

probes.intro: In this chapter of The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Bertrand Russell asks what makes a true belief count as knowledge. His examples refer to British prime ministers and newspapers of his day.

items.stem: Why does Russell reject defining knowledge simply as “true belief”?
options: No belief can ever be completely true
A belief can be true by luck or come from a false belief
Knowledge needs an official source, such as a telegram report
True beliefs are always reached by valid reasoning
items.rationale: Readers of a lucky newspaper forecast believe the right result, but “they cannot be said to have knowledge.”

items.stem: What does the example about Socrates being a Greek illustrate?
options: False premisses can still make a perfectly valid argument
Historical facts about the life of Socrates are uncertain
A true conclusion is not knowledge if it does not follow
Intuitive knowledge cannot be defined
items.rationale: Though premisses and conclusion are true, “the conclusion does not follow from the premisses.”

items.stem: Why does Russell call the definition “knowledge is what is validly deduced from known premisses” circular?
options: It uses the idea of knowing to define knowing
It returns at the end to the example it began with
It covers too many cases
It depends on a false belief
items.rationale: He says “it assumes that we already know what is meant by” known premisses.

items.stem: What does Russell conclude about the idea of knowledge at the end of the passage?
options: It can be defined exactly as deduction from known premisses
It is the same thing as true belief
It applies only to intuitive knowledge
It is not precise and shades into probable opinion
items.rationale: “knowledge” “is not a precise conception: it merges into” probable opinion.
